In [[abstract algebra]], '''Kaplansky's theorem on projective modules''', first proven by [[Irving Kaplansky]], states that a [[projective module]] over a [[local ring#General case|local ring]] is [[free module|free]];<ref name="theorem">{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=Corollary 26.7.}}</ref> where a not-necessarily-commutative ring is called ''local'' if for each element ''x'', either ''x'' or 1 &minus; ''x'' is a unit element.<ref>{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=Proposition 15.15.}}</ref> The theorem can also be formulated so to characterize a local ring ([[#Characterization of a local ring]]).

For a [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]] projective module over a commutative local ring, the theorem is an easy consequence of [[Nakayama's lemma]].<ref>{{harvnb|Matsumura|1989|loc=Theorem 2.5.}}</ref> For the general case, the proof (both the original as well as later one) consists of the following two steps:
*Observe that a projective module over an arbitrary ring is a direct sum of [[countably generated module|countably generated]] projective modules.
*Show that a countably generated projective module over a local ring is free (by a "[reminiscence] of the proof of Nakayama's lemma"<ref>{{harvnb|Lam|2000|loc=Part 1. § 1.}}</ref>).

The idea of the proof of the theorem was also later used by [[Hyman Bass]] to show [[big projective modules]] (under some mild conditions) are free.<ref>{{harvnb|Bass|1963}}</ref> According to {{harv|Anderson|Fuller|1992}}, Kaplansky's theorem "is very likely the inspiration for a major portion of the results" in the theory of [[semiperfect ring]]s.<ref name="theorem" />

== Proof ==
The proof of the theorem is based on two lemmas, both of which concern decompositions of modules and are of independent general interest.

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma 1|math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=Theorem 26.1.}}</ref> Let <math>\mathfrak{F}</math> denote the family of modules that are direct sums of some countably generated submodules (here modules can be those over a ring, a group or even a set of endomorphisms). If <math>M</math> is in <math>\mathfrak{F}</math>, then each direct summand of <math>M</math> is also in <math>\mathfrak{F}</math>.}}

''Proof'': Let ''N'' be a direct summand; i.e., <math>M = N \oplus L</math>. Using the assumption, we write <math>M = \bigoplus_{i \in I} M_i</math> where each <math>M_i</math> is a countably generated submodule. For each subset <math>A \subset I</math>, we write <math>M_A = \bigoplus_{i \in A} M_i, N_A =</math> the image of <math>M_A</math> under the projection <math>M \to N \hookrightarrow M</math> and <math>L_A</math> the same way. Now, consider the set of all triples (<math>J</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math>) consisting of a subset <math>J \subset I</math> and subsets <math>B, C \subset \mathfrak{F}</math> such that <math>M_J = N_J \oplus L_J</math> and <math>N_J, L_J</math> are the direct sums of the modules in <math>B, C</math>. We give this set a partial ordering such that <math>(J, B, C) \le (J', B', C')</math> if and only if <math>J \subset J'</math>, <math>B \subset B', C \subset C'</math>. By [[Zorn's lemma]], the set contains a maximal element <math>(J, B, C)</math>. We shall show that <math>J = I</math>; i.e., <math>N = N_J = \bigoplus_{N' \in B} N' \in \mathfrak{F}</math>. Suppose otherwise. Then we can inductively construct a sequence of at most countable subsets <math>I_1 \subset I_2 \subset \cdots \subset I</math> such that <math>I_1 \not\subset J</math> and for each integer <math>n \ge 1</math>,
:<math>M_{I_n} \subset N_{I_n} + L_{I_n} \subset M_{I_{n+1}}</math>.
Let <math>I' = \bigcup_0^\infty I_n</math> and <math>J' = J \cup I'</math>. We claim:
:<math>M_{J'} = N_{J'} \oplus L_{J'}.</math>
The inclusion <math>\subset</math> is trivial. Conversely, <math>N_{J'}</math> is the image of <math>N_J + L_J + M_{I'} \subset N_J + M_{I'}</math> and so <math>N_{J'} \subset M_{J'}</math>. The same is also true for <math>L_{J'}</math>. Hence,  the claim is valid.

Now, <math>N_J</math> is a direct summand of <math>M</math> (since it is a summand of <math>M_J</math>, which is a summand of <math>M</math>); i.e., <math>N_J \oplus M' = M</math> for some <math>M'</math>. Then, by modular law, <math>N_{J'} = N_J \oplus (M' \cap N_{J'})</math>. Set <math>\widetilde{N_J} = M' \cap N_{J'}</math>. Define <math>\widetilde{L_J}</math> in the same way. Then, using the early claim, we have:
:<math>M_{J'} = M_J \oplus \widetilde{N_J} \oplus \widetilde{L_J},</math>
which implies that
:<math>\widetilde{N_J} \oplus \widetilde{L_J} \simeq M_{J'} / M_J \simeq M_{J' - J}</math>
is countably generated as <math>J' - J \subset I'</math>. This contradicts the maximality of <math>(J, B, C)</math>. <math>\square</math>

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma 2|math_statement=If <math>M_i, i \in I</math> are countably generated modules with local endomorphism rings and if <math>N</math> is a countably generated module that is a direct summand of <math>\bigoplus_{i \in I} M_i</math>, then <math>N</math> is isomorphic to <math>\bigoplus_{i \in I'} M_i</math> for some at most countable subset <math>I' \subset I</math>.}}

''Proof'':<ref>{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=Proof of Theorem 26.5.}}</ref> Let <math>\mathcal{G}</math> denote the family of modules that are isomorphic to modules of the form <math>\bigoplus_{i \in F} M_i</math> for some finite subset <math>F \subset I</math>. The assertion is then implied by the following claim:
*Given an element <math>x \in N</math>, there exists an <math>H \in \mathcal{G}</math> that contains ''x'' and is a direct summand of&nbsp;''N''.
Indeed, assume the claim is valid. Then choose a sequence <math>x_1, x_2, \dots</math> in ''N'' that is a generating set. Then using the claim, write <math>N = H_1 \oplus N_1</math> where <math>x_1 \in H_1 \in \mathcal{G}</math>. Then we write <math>x_2 = y + z</math> where <math>y \in H_1, z \in N_1</math>. We then decompose <math>N_1 = H_2 \oplus N_2</math> with <math>z \in H_2 \in \mathcal{G}</math>. Note <math>\{ x_1, x_2 \} \subset H_1 \oplus H_2</math>. Repeating this argument, in the end, we have: <math display="inline"> \{ x_1, x_2, \dots \} \subset \bigoplus_0^\infty H_n</math>; i.e., <math display="inline">N = \bigoplus_0^\infty H_n</math>. Hence, the proof reduces to proving the claim and the claim is a straightforward consequence of [[Azumaya's theorem]] (see the linked article for the argument). <math>\square</math>

''Proof of the theorem'': Let <math>N</math> be a projective module over a local ring. Then, by definition, it is a direct summand of some free module <math>F</math>. This <math>F</math> is in the family <math>\mathfrak{F}</math> in Lemma 1; thus, <math>N</math> is a direct sum of countably generated submodules, each a direct summand of ''F'' and thus projective. Hence, without loss of generality, we can assume <math>N</math> is countably generated. Then Lemma 2 gives the theorem. <math>\square</math>

== Characterization of a local ring ==
Kaplansky's theorem can be stated in such a way to give a characterization of a local ring. A direct summand is said to be ''maximal'' if it has an indecomposable complement.

{{math_theorem|math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=Exercise 26.3.}}</ref> Let ''R'' be a ring. Then the following are equivalent.
# ''R'' is a local ring.
# Every projective module over ''R'' is free and has an [[indecomposable decomposition]] <math>M = \bigoplus_{i \in I} M_i</math> such that for each maximal direct summand ''L'' of ''M'', there is a decomposition <math>M = \Big(\bigoplus_{j \in J} M_j\Big) \bigoplus L</math> for some subset <math>J \subset I</math>.}}

The implication <math>1. \Rightarrow 2.</math> is exactly (usual) Kaplansky's theorem and Azumaya's theorem. The converse <math>2. \Rightarrow 1.</math> follows from the following general fact, which is interesting itself:

*A ring ''R'' is local <math>\Leftrightarrow</math> for each nonzero proper direct summand ''M'' of <math>R^2 = R \times R</math>, either <math>R^2 = (0 \times R) \oplus M</math> or <math>R^2 = (R \times 0) \oplus M</math>.

<math>(\Rightarrow)</math> is by Azumaya's theorem as in the proof of <math>1. \Rightarrow 2.</math>. Conversely, suppose <math>R^2</math> has the above property and that an element ''x'' in ''R'' is given. Consider the linear map <math>\sigma:R^2 \to R, \, \sigma(a, b) = a - b</math>. Set <math>y = x - 1</math>. Then <math>\sigma(x, y) = 1</math>, which is to say <math>\eta: R \to R^2, a \mapsto (ax, ay)</math> splits and the image <math>M</math> is a direct summand of <math>R^2</math>. It follows easily from that the assumption that either ''x'' or -''y'' is a unit element. <math>\square</math>
